note: Erkundung auf dem Platz vor der Großen Halle während der Parade (Kapitel 2, Konrad). Konrads Stimme: genau, beschönigend, mit jedem Fund brüchiger; nie feierlich. Daten: data/explore/plaza.json.

strings.explore.plaza.tram_stop.title: The 74 tram stop
strings.explore.plaza.tram_stop.text: The stop for the 74, closed “until the completion of the axis”. Below it a new notice, neatly typed: special services for resettlers from grid squares Süd seven to twelve, from the West goods station, loading ramp three, luggage at most two hundredweight per family. A goods station is there for goods. I read the word “resettlers” again and can find no point at which it stops being just a word.
strings.explore.plaza.poster.title: The parade poster
strings.explore.plaza.poster.text: On the poster column: “One People. One Order. One Square.” Below it the Great Hall in silhouette, the national emblem over the dome and, in small print, the programme: 10:00 assembly, 11:00 march-past of the formations, 17:00 cathedral of light. In the corner someone has written a house number in pencil and rubbed it out again. You can still see it. I read it twice before I notice that I am memorising it.
strings.explore.plaza.vendor.title: The chestnut man
strings.explore.plaza.vendor.text: An old man roasts chestnuts in a drum that was once a stovepipe. On his board: “Chestnuts 30 Pf. Children with red noses 20 Pf.” He examines every nose with a serious look and always decides in the child’s favour. He folds the bags from old city maps; mine holds a piece of Moabit with streets that no longer exist. I pocketed the bag anyway. The chestnuts were good.
strings.explore.plaza.loudspeaker.title: The loudspeaker mast
strings.explore.plaza.loudspeaker.text: Three horns on a mast, aimed over the heads in three directions. Between announcements a voice lists divisions, regiments and districts of origin, as if reading out an inventory. Then the gong: “Attendance is being recorded.” I know the masts from the cabling plan, cable cross-section and spacing, one every forty metres. Forty metres, so that nobody on this square can say they did not hear it.
strings.explore.plaza.children.title: Two children on a crate
strings.explore.plaza.children.text: Two children stand on a fruit crate to see over the heads. The boy waves a paper flag that was handed out at the entrance, in time with the boots, so earnestly that the grown-ups laugh. His little sister waves nothing. She catches snowflakes on her tongue and nearly loses her balance. I catch myself wishing she may never learn to keep in step.
strings.explore.plaza.barrier.title: The barrier
strings.explore.plaza.barrier.text: Wooden trestles, painted red and white, linked by chains; on every third one a sign: “Reorganisation District – Line Up by House Number”. The people behind them really are lined up by house number, even on the left, odd on the right, like a card index. A man in plain clothes walks along the row with a clipboard, ticking them off. Nobody cheers. Nobody leaves. I notice I am checking my own posture, as if I too were on a list.
strings.explore.plaza.guard.title: The sentry
strings.explore.plaza.guard.text: The sentry behind the barrier is barely twenty. His helmet shades his eyes, his rifle is at the order, and he looks not at the tanks but at the residents, as he has been ordered to. When a child waves to him, his hand twitches on the sling, then stays down. I drew the passage just wide enough for a single man to hold it. I did not think of his age.
strings.explore.plaza.tank.title: The parked tank
strings.explore.plaza.tank.text: Where there was a back courtyard until the summer, a tank now stands, parked for the march-past, snow on its hull. One of the crew warms himself at a fire barrel and smokes as if he were on a building site. Next to the track, a carpet-beating rail juts out of the rubble, bent but upright. I designated this area as a marshalling space for heavy equipment, checked load capacity and turning radius. On my plan there was only white here.
strings.explore.plaza.tribune.title: The reviewing stand
strings.explore.plaza.tribune.text: The reviewing stand is exactly where I drew it in 1958: centre of the axis, twelve steps, angle of view to the dome no less than thirty degrees. Back then it was a question of sightlines. Today men in fur collars stand there saluting, and their sightline ends at the barrier, behind which the residents of the cleared blocks are freezing. That was in my plan too. There it was simply called “open space”.
strings.explore.plaza.banner.title: The banners
strings.explore.plaza.banner.text: The banners on the façades are twenty metres long; I know because the hooks are in our façade plan, three metres twenty apart, load capacity checked. In the wind they beat against the windows of houses that are already empty. In one a curtain still hangs, gathered to one side from within, as if someone were about to come home. The flag in front of it is bigger than the whole flat.
strings.explore.plaza.rubble.title: Rubble from block Süd 8
strings.explore.plaza.rubble.text: On the fire wall left standing you can still see the stairs, the storeys and the wallpaper of the rooms, like a section in my plans. In front of it the rubble, neatly heaped into cones: wallpaper with blue roses, a stove tile, a doorbell plate with no name. And a cloth badge, blue and white: OST. The demolition gangs wear it on their chests. I saw them every morning and never asked who pays them. I suppose: no one.
strings.explore.plaza.family_door.title: The sealed front door
strings.explore.plaza.family_door.text: House number nine, grid square Süd 8. Two battens across the door, a seal strip with red wax over the lock, and beside it the eviction order: vacate by the fourteenth, household goods up to two hundredweight per family, replacement housing “will be allocated”. It was signed by a head of department from our building; I know him from the lunch table. In front of it stand a woman, a man with a crate and a child, watching the parade, because their attendance is being recorded.
strings.explore.plaza.window.title: The window on the third floor
strings.explore.plaza.window.text: On the third floor opposite the sealed door, a lamp burns behind the curtain. A woman stands there, looking not at the parade but at the family below. When she notices me looking up, she draws the curtain, slowly, without haste. A plate remains on the windowsill, a cloth over it, as if waiting for someone who may fetch it once the square is empty.
strings.explore.plaza.photographer.title: The press photographer
strings.explore.plaza.photographer.text: A press photographer explains which pictures may appear in tomorrow’s paper – and which he takes all the same.
strings.explore.plaza.photographer.l1: One step to the left, sir, you’re in my shot. No, not you – the people behind you.
strings.explore.plaza.photographer.l2: The residents behind the barrier? Surely they’re part of the square.
strings.explore.plaza.photographer.l3: Not on my plates. Orders from above: tanks, grandstand, dome, cheering youth. Tomorrow there are no barriers.
strings.explore.plaza.photographer.l4: And if someone does push into the picture?
strings.explore.plaza.photographer.l5: Then it gets retouched. I know a colleague who can turn a crowd into paving in twenty minutes.
strings.explore.plaza.photographer.l6: You photograph the people anyway. I saw you turn the camera.
strings.explore.plaza.photographer.l7: One plate for the paper, one for the drawer. Somebody has to know what it really looked like. You’re from the building office, aren’t you? You’d know best.
strings.explore.plaza.photographer.l8: I know what it was supposed to look like. That’s not the same.
strings.explore.plaza.neighbour.title: The woman from number nine
strings.explore.plaza.neighbour.text: A woman from the cleared block waits with her husband, child and suitcase in front of her old door until their attendance has been recorded.
strings.explore.plaza.neighbour.l1: Excuse me. Do you live here?
strings.explore.plaza.neighbour.l2: Until the fourteenth. Now we’re standing here because they want us counted. Afterwards we may go. Where to is on a slip we haven’t got yet.
strings.explore.plaza.neighbour.l3: The replacement housing will be allocated. It is an orderly procedure.
strings.explore.plaza.neighbour.l4: That’s what the gentleman with the clipboard says too. He says it very kindly.
strings.explore.plaza.neighbour.l5: My husband helped rebuild the house after the bombs, stone by stone. Now it’s an open space. That’s what it’s called, isn’t it? You look as if you’d know what it’s called.
strings.explore.plaza.neighbour.l7: The little one thinks the tanks are driving past for her sake. I let her. It’s easier than the truth.
strings.explore.plaza.neighbour.l8: I hope the new flat is warm.
strings.explore.plaza.neighbour.l9: You go on hoping that, sir. Somebody has to.
strings.char.photographer.name: Press photographer
strings.explore.plaza.frost_heart.title: Heart in the frost
strings.explore.plaza.frost_heart.text: On the lamp post someone has breathed a heart into the hoarfrost and traced it with a glove, with “H + G” inside. Below it, smaller and in a different hand: “About time.” I examined the letters the way I usually examine signatures and could not work out who H is or who G is. Nor did I look any further. It is the first thing today that I have no wish to transfer to any file. By tomorrow morning it will have melted, and that is all right.
strings.explore.plaza.leaflet.title: The sheet in the snow
strings.explore.plaza.leaflet.text: A carbon copy, typewritten, the ribbon almost dry. At the top, in capitals: “WHO IS MISSING?” Below it, names, house numbers, floors, block by block, in the order of our clearance list, only without file numbers. Someone in the office has copied out what I signed off. At the bottom, in pencil: “Please pass on.” I should have handed it in. It is now in my inside pocket, next to my service pass.
strings.explore.plaza.paws.title: Tracks in the snow
strings.explore.plaza.paws.text: Paw prints, neatly placed one behind the other: out from under the barrier, across the pavement, past all the boots to the chestnut man’s cart. A cat. It had no pass, no cockade and quite obviously no hurry. Now it lies under the cart, where the embers melt the snow, with its eyes closed. Of everyone on this square it has the best place, and it did not let anyone allocate it.
